title: Identifying Neural State Changes due to Gain versus Off-Manifold Displacement
summary: Memory segmentation is thought to arise from rapid decorrelation in neural activity, often quantified by Euclidean distance or cosine angle. Although these metrics detect a transition, they do not reveal how the new state relates to the repertoire represented by the neural manifold. This matters because neuromodulators that drive state transitions also alter excitability, and learning may repurpose existing representations or create new ones. Here, I introduce a geometric decomposition that separates changes attributable to gain modulation of a nearby manifold state from movement within the manifold and genuine off-manifold displacement. The approach uses the radial axis of neural population activity to partition the normal space of a local manifold region. A central challenge is identifiability: given only a static reference manifold and a single test state, neither the state from which a perturbation began nor its gain magnitude and mechanistic decomposition can generally be recovered uniquely. I therefore formulate identifiability as a cascade of geometric gates specifying when each component can be interpreted. The gates distinguish structural failures, including the absence of a local chart or incorrect intrinsic dimensionality, from estimation error and systematic bias caused by reference sampling, tangent-frame error, gain-axis misalignment, anchor displacement, and poor ratio conditioning. Simulations show that neighborhood size, curvature, sampling density, ambient dimension, and noise act through a small set of geometric quantities. The framework specifies when assignments to gain or novelty are identifiable, how they become biased, and which diagnostics reveal the relevant failure regime. By quantifying the nature rather than only the magnitude of neural state change, it provides a clear, readily interpretable framework for evaluating mechanisms of neural state transitions.

AI.tldr: Introduces a geometric decomposition of neural state changes into gain modulation, within-manifold movement, and off-manifold novelty, with identifiability analysis via geometric gates.
AI.motivation: Existing metrics (Euclidean distance, cosine angle) detect neural state transitions but fail to reveal how a new state relates to the neural manifold's repertoire. This matters because neuromodulators driving transitions also change excitability, and learning may repurpose or create representations.
AI.method: A geometric decomposition using the radial axis of population activity to partition the normal space of a local manifold region, separating gain modulation of a nearby manifold state from within-manifold movement and genuine off-manifold displacement. Identifiability is formulated as a cascade of geometric gates distinguishing structural failures (missing local chart, wrong intrinsic dimensionality) from estimation error and systematic bias (reference sampling, tangent-frame error, gain-axis misalignment, anchor displacement, poor ratio conditioning).
AI.result: Simulations show neighborhood size, curvature, sampling density, ambient dimension, and noise act through a small set of geometric quantities. The framework specifies when gain vs. novelty assignments are identifiable, how they become biased, and which diagnostics reveal the failure regime.
AI.conclusion: By quantifying the nature, not just magnitude, of neural state change, the framework offers a clear, interpretable tool for evaluating mechanisms of neural state transitions.

title: High Reconstruction Quality and Restart Repeatability Do Not Guarantee Recovery of Ground-Truth Muscle Synergies
comment: 29 pages, 4 figures, 1 table; includes a technical appendix
summary: High reconstruction quality and agreement across repeated fits do not necessarily establish recovery of muscle synergies. We tested whether a variance-accounted-for (VAF)/elbow rule recovers the generating synergy count and spatial vectors, whether high restart repeatability indicates recovery, and how five design factors affect recovery. Non-negative matrix factorisation was applied to 4,320 synthetic 16-muscle datasets varying generating rank, noise, trial count, spatial similarity and activation overlap. Combined recovery required the correct rank and cosine similarity of at least 0.80 for every matched spatial vector. Factor effects and two-factor interactions were assessed using exploratory heteroscedastic Wald tests with Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment. Rank selection was exact in 17.6% of datasets, too low in 54.9% and too high in 27.5%; combined recovery was 13.9%. Among fits with VAF at least 0.90, only 11.3% achieved combined recovery. Among 3,762 datasets with spatial repeatability at least 0.95, 19.6% had the correct rank and 15.7% achieved combined recovery. All five factors were associated with recovery (adjusted p < 0.001). Recovery declined from 26.2% to 1.7% with increasing spatial similarity and from 26.2% to 2.2% with increasing activation overlap. It was lower at ranks 7-9 than at 3-5, increased from 11.0% with 3 trials to 15.8% with 80 trials, and varied non-monotonically with noise. Five noiseless signals synthesised from measured-sEMG reference factors also showed under-selection despite VAF above 0.918. Under this selector, high reconstruction quality and restart agreement were insufficient indicators of correct rank and spatial recovery. Muscle-synergy interpretation should account for rank sensitivity and the separability of spatial and activation patterns.

AI.tldr: High reconstruction quality (VAF) and repeatable fits do not guarantee correct recovery of muscle synergies; a VAF/elbow rule frequently misestimates rank and spatial vectors, and recovery is influenced by five design factors.
AI.motivation: Researchers often assume that high VAF and consistent results across repeated fits establish successful muscle synergy recovery. This study questions that assumption, testing whether these conventional indicators truly reflect recovery of the generating synergy count and spatial vectors.
AI.method: NMF was applied to 4,320 synthetic 16-muscle datasets varying five factors: generating rank, noise, trial count, spatial similarity, and activation overlap. Recovery required correct rank plus cosine similarity ≥0.80 for every matched spatial vector. Factor effects and two-factor interactions were tested with exploratory heteroscedastic Wald tests and Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment.
AI.result: Rank selection was exact in only 17.6% (too low 54.9%, too high 27.5%); combined recovery was 13.9%. Among fits with VAF ≥0.90, only 11.3% achieved combined recovery. Among datasets with spatial repeatability ≥0.95, only 15.7% achieved combined recovery. All five factors affected recovery (adjusted p<0.001). Noiseless signals from measured-sEMG reference factors also showed under-selection despite VAF >0.918.
AI.conclusion: Under this selector, high reconstruction quality and restart agreement are insufficient indicators of correct rank and spatial recovery. Muscle-synergy interpretation should account for rank sensitivity and the separability of spatial and activation patterns.

title: Best Matches in Phylogenetic Networks
summary: Best match graphs (BMGs) were introduced in mathematical phylogenetics to describe the concept of closest relatives for related genes (leaves of rooted tree) in different organisms (defining leaf colors). We generalize this concept here to leaf-colored rooted networks, where least common ancestors are in general neither unique nor comparable. We characterize BMGs of rooted networks as those vertex-colored digraphs that are properly colored and satisfy an easy-to-check condition that we call the sicor-in-hub property. BMGs can be recognized in linear time and an explaining network can be constructed in quadratic time. Analogous results are obtained for reciprocal best match graphs (RBMGs), where an edge $\{x,y\}$ corresponds to pairs of vertices with different color that are mutually closest relatives.

AI.tldr: The paper generalizes best match graphs (BMGs) from rooted trees to leaf-colored rooted networks, characterizing them via the sicor-in-hub property, and provides recognition and construction algorithms.
AI.motivation: BMGs were originally defined in mathematical phylogenetics for rooted trees to capture closest relatives among genes (leaves) from different organisms (leaf colors). This concept is generalized to rooted networks, where least common ancestors are generally neither unique nor comparable.
AI.method: The authors extend BMGs to leaf-colored rooted networks and characterize them as vertex-colored digraphs that are properly colored and satisfy the sicor-in-hub property, an easy-to-check condition.
AI.result: BMGs can be recognized in linear time, and an explaining network can be constructed in quadratic time. Analogous results are obtained for reciprocal best match graphs (RBMGs), where an edge links differently colored vertices that are mutually closest relatives.
AI.conclusion: The concept of BMGs extends naturally to rooted networks, with efficient recognition and construction algorithms, and analogous results hold for RBMGs.

title: Exact Counts of Binary Phylogenetic Networks with Four Reticulations
summary:
Phylogenetic networks provide a flexible framework for representing reticulate evolutionary processes, such as hybridization, introgression, recombination, and horizontal gene transfer. However, their combinatorial complexity makes even basic enumeration problems difficult. Building on our previous work for networks with up to three reticulations, we derive an explicit closed-form formula for the number of unrestricted rooted binary phylogenetic networks with four reticulations on \(n\) labeled taxa.
  Our approach is based on tree-component graphs. We classify the 79 possible component graphs corresponding to networks with four reticulations into ten groups. We then enumerate the networks associated with each group by combining known counts of one-component networks, forests, and networks with fewer reticulations. Summing these contributions yields the desired formula. This result extends the exact enumeration of unrestricted binary phylogenetic networks to four reticulations and further demonstrates the effectiveness of component graphs for systematically organizing and counting increasingly complex network classes.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a closed-form formula for the number of unrestricted rooted binary phylogenetic networks with four reticulations on n labeled taxa, using a tree-component-graph classification method.
AI.motivation: Phylogenetic networks model reticulate evolution (hybridization, recombination, etc.), but their combinatorial complexity makes even basic enumeration hard. Prior work only handled up to three reticulations.
AI.method: Use tree-component graphs: classify the 79 possible component graphs for four-reticulation networks into ten groups, then enumerate networks per group by combining known counts of one-component networks, forests, and networks with fewer reticulations.
AI.result: An explicit closed-form formula for the number of unrestricted rooted binary phylogenetic networks with four reticulations on n labeled taxa, obtained by summing the contributions across the ten component-graph groups.
AI.conclusion: The result extends exact enumeration of unrestricted binary phylogenetic networks to four reticulations and demonstrates the effectiveness of component graphs for systematically organizing and counting increasingly complex network classes.

title: Retention-Constrained Post-Training Quantization of Cellpose-SAM for Stem Cell Microscopy
comment: Peer-reviewed and accepted at NeurIPS 2026 LXAI Workshop. Pending presentation/publication at JLXAIR
summary: Induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) culture increasingly relies on segmentation foundation models, yet deployment on laboratory CPUs and edge hardware requires compression schemes that are both efficient and auditable. We present a deployment-oriented evaluation of compressed Cellpose-SAM using a pre-specified retention criterion: the 95% cluster-bootstrap interval of mean change from FP32 must remain above a fixed -0.02 margin for every imaging modality. On a stratified 176-field panel spanning BBBC038 nuclei, BBBC039 U2OS fluorescence, and NIST iPSC images across density regimes, weight-only W8A16 preserves instance F1 across all modalities. A sensitivity-guided mixed W4/W8 scheme, using four INT8 exceptions, achieves a 6.76x reduction in weight storage with no observed catastrophic failures (0/176 fields), matching W8A16 at this sample size. In contrast, ternary weight-only quantization achieves 12.08x compression but fails catastrophically on 169/176 fields. These results demonstrate that compression should be evaluated by modality-stratified downstream retention rather than single-number accuracy, and establish a reproducible protocol for auditing compressed foundation models in regulated stem-cell imaging.

AI.tldr: Deployment-oriented evaluation of compressed Cellpose-SAM for iPSC imaging, showing weight-only W8A16 and a sensitivity-guided mixed W4/W8 scheme preserve instance F1, while ternary quantization fails catastrophically.
AI.motivation: iPSC culture increasingly relies on segmentation foundation models, but deployment on laboratory CPUs and edge hardware needs compression that is both efficient and auditable. Single-number accuracy is insufficient for regulated stem-cell imaging.
AI.method: Pre-specified retention criterion: the 95% cluster-bootstrap interval of mean change from FP32 must stay above a -0.02 margin for every imaging modality. Evaluated on a stratified 176-field panel spanning BBBC038 nuclei, BBBC039 U2OS fluorescence, and NIST iPSC images across density regimes. Compared weight-only W8A16, a sensitivity-guided mixed W4/W8 scheme with four INT8 exceptions, and ternary weight-only quantization.
AI.result: W8A16 preserves instance F1 across all modalities. Mixed W4/W8 achieves 6.76x weight storage reduction with no observed catastrophic failures (0/176 fields), matching W8A16 at this sample size. Ternary quantization achieves 12.08x compression but fails catastrophically on 169/176 fields.
AI.conclusion: Compression should be evaluated by modality-stratified downstream retention rather than single-number accuracy. The work establishes a reproducible protocol for auditing compressed foundation models in regulated stem-cell imaging.

title: Hybrid quantum-classical attention for histopathology-based molecular profiling in data-limited cancers
summary: Molecular profiling from routine histopathology could expand access to precision oncology when sequencing is unavailable, tissue is limited, or training cohorts are small. We developed a hybrid quantum-classical strategy that replaces softmax attention in a transformer for histopathology-based gene expression prediction with a quantum-derived doubly stochastic matrix (QDSM). Across 29 cancer cohorts from The Cancer Genome Atlas and an independent pancreatic cancer cohort from the Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium, QDSM attention produced selective gains, with the largest relative improvements in smaller, data-limited cohorts, including adrenocortical carcinoma and uveal melanoma. Rather than improving transcriptome-wide performance uniformly, QDSM redistributed predictive accuracy across genes and pathways, improving biologically relevant targets in some tumor contexts while worsening others. In adrenocortical carcinoma, preferentially improved genes were enriched for adverse overall-survival associations, linking enhanced molecular inference to prognostically relevant biology. In pancreatic cancer transfer experiments, QDSM improved selected metabolic and lineage-associated genes but did not consistently improve performance under cross-cohort shift. Leave-one-cancer-out mixed-effects analysis showed that baseline molecular features predicted part of the gene-level benefit, while residuals identified cancer-specific programs that improved more or less than expected. Separate experiments on IBM quantum processors recovered the doubly stochastic matrix primitive underlying the attention mechanism. These findings position QDSM attention as a context- and target-dependent strategy for image-based molecular profiling and molecular triage when direct testing is unavailable, incomplete, or impractical.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces QDSM attention, a hybrid quantum-classical replacement for softmax attention in transformers, for predicting gene expression from histopathology images. It shows context- and target-dependent gains rather than uniform improvements.
AI.motivation: Molecular profiling is often inaccessible due to limited sequencing availability, limited tissue, or small training cohorts. Predicting gene expression from routine histopathology could broaden precision oncology access, but standard softmax attention may not optimally capture relevant structure.
AI.method: A hybrid quantum-classical strategy replaces softmax attention in a histopathology transformer with a quantum-derived doubly stochastic matrix (QDSM). Evaluated across 29 TCGA cancer cohorts plus an independent CPTAC pancreatic cancer cohort, with leave-one-cancer-out mixed-effects analysis and transfer experiments. The doubly stochastic matrix primitive was also recovered on IBM quantum processors.
AI.result: QDSM attention produced selective gains, largest in smaller, data-limited cohorts (e.g., adrenocortical carcinoma, uveal melanoma). It redistributed accuracy across genes/pathways rather than improving transcriptome-wide performance uniformly. In adrenocortical carcinoma, improved genes were enriched for adverse survival associations. In pancreatic cancer transfer, gains were inconsistent under cross-cohort shift. Baseline molecular features predicted part of the gene-level benefit.
AI.conclusion: QDSM attention is a context- and target-dependent strategy for image-based molecular profiling and molecular triage when direct testing is unavailable, incomplete, or impractical.

title: Reliability-Centered Evaluation of Sparse Longitudinal CT Lesion-Size Forecasting with Conformal Interval Calibration and Gompertz-Inspired Regularization
summary: Sparse longitudinal CT follow-up limits lesion-size forecasting when only a few prior observations are available. We constructed a five-visit DLT-derived same-lesion trajectory benchmark from DeepLesion and Deep Lesion Tracker (DLT), yielding 205 trajectories from 129 patients. We compared an exploratory conventional sparse-to-final analysis with a primary fixed visit-index horizon design predicting the common log change from T3 to T4 while progressively adding earlier observations, evaluating predictive accuracy, uncertainty reliability, post-hoc conformal interval calibration, subgroup performance, and Gompertz-inspired trajectory regularization. The evaluated methods showed partially overlapping point-prediction accuracy but distinct uncertainty behavior. Mean held-out RMSE across ten training seeds was 0.4726, 0.4305, 0.4499, and 0.4513 for m = 1, 2, 3, 4, indicating the lowest mean RMSE at m = 2; additional history did not improve RMSE. At m = 4, raw Cohort-Level Feature GP coverage was near the 95% nominal level, whereas MC Dropout, Deep Ensemble, and residual-scale intervals were conservative. Patient-level conformal calibration generally produced near-nominal or conservative coverage at the cost of wider intervals. Patient-grouped development cross-validation selected lambda* = 0 for the Gompertz-inspired term. A global population reference frequently opposed lesion-level change directions, and prediction difficulty varied across anatomical subgroups. Overall, additional historical observations provided limited predictive benefit once the prediction horizon was controlled, while predictive accuracy, uncertainty reliability, and trajectory consistency did not necessarily improve together, and should be evaluated jointly in sparse longitudinal imaging.

AI.tldr: A five-visit same-lesion CT trajectory benchmark (205 trajectories, 129 patients) shows that adding more prior observations gives limited forecasting benefit once the prediction horizon is fixed, and accuracy, uncertainty reliability, and trajectory consistency do not improve together.
AI.motivation: Sparse longitudinal CT follow-up limits lesion-size forecasting when few prior observations exist, so there is a need to understand how predictive accuracy, uncertainty reliability, and trajectory consistency behave jointly as more history is added under a controlled horizon.
AI.method: Built a five-visit DLT-derived same-lesion trajectory benchmark from DeepLesion and DLT. Compared an exploratory sparse-to-final analysis with a primary fixed visit-index design predicting the common log change from T3 to T4 while progressively adding earlier observations. Evaluated point accuracy, uncertainty reliability, post-hoc conformal calibration, subgroup performance, and Gompertz-inspired regularization, plus patient-grouped development cross-validation.
AI.result: Mean held-out RMSE across ten seeds was 0.4726, 0.4305, 0.4499, 0.4513 for m=1,2,3,4, lowest at m=2. At m=4, raw Cohort-Level Feature GP coverage neared 95%, while MC Dropout, Deep Ensemble, and residual-scale intervals were conservative. Patient-level conformal calibration gave near-nominal or conservative coverage but wider intervals. CV selected lambda*=0 for the Gompertz term. A global population reference often opposed lesion-level change, and difficulty varied by anatomical subgroup.
AI.conclusion: Additional historical observations gave limited predictive benefit once the horizon was controlled; accuracy, uncertainty reliability, and trajectory consistency should be evaluated jointly in sparse longitudinal imaging.

title: Compartmental Epidemiological Models: Discussing Fundamental Elements via the SIR Model
summary: We present a didactic treatment of compartmental disease spread modeling centered on the SIR framework, aimed at mathematics education. Our focus is on how modeling choices encode transmission mechanisms and data-collection practices. We begin by stating the structural hypotheses of compartmental models, including population partitioning, homogeneous mixing, flow closure, and Markovian transitions. We then derive the basic SIR dynamic equations in both continuous-time (differential equations) and discrete-time (difference equations) settings. A key goal is to clarify the distinction between density-dependent and frequency-dependent transmission. We do this by constructing the force of infection from the contact rate, prevalence, and per-contact transmissibility while tracking units and interpretations. We go beyond the usual mass-balance SIR model by introducing the discrete Kermack-McKendrick perspective through the cumulative force of infection. This naturally leads to discrete SIR updates with an exponential escape probability term. We also derive Bernoulli-based exponential formulations for both density- and frequency-dependent transmission, interpret these probabilistically over observation intervals, and obtain the associated discrete infectivity kernel. This highlights how geometric infectious survival emerges from per-step removal. The paper includes reproducible, introductory-level Python code to implement the basic discrete SIR model, the continuous SIR model, and the exponential discrete variants. We provide instructors with an example of parameter estimation from prevalence data using least squares, along with guidance on interpretation and limitations. This framework is designed to help teachers integrate model assumptions, units, simulation, and inference in a coherent introduction to infectious disease modeling.

AI.tldr: A didactic treatment of compartmental SIR modeling for mathematics education, clarifying modeling assumptions, density- vs frequency-dependent transmission, and discrete Kermack-McKendrick formulations with reproducible Python code.
AI.motivation: Compartmental disease models are widely taught but their structural assumptions, unit tracking, and the distinction between transmission types are often glossed over, leaving students unclear on how modeling choices encode mechanisms and data practices.
AI.method: States structural hypotheses (partitioning, homogeneous mixing, flow closure, Markovian transitions); derives continuous- and discrete-time SIR equations; constructs force of infection from contact rate, prevalence, and transmissibility; introduces discrete Kermack-McKendrick via cumulative force of infection; derives Bernoulli-based exponential formulations and discrete infectivity kernel; implements in introductory Python.
AI.result: Yields discrete SIR updates with exponential escape probability, both density- and frequency-dependent variants, a geometric infectious survival interpretation, reproducible code for three model types, and an example parameter estimation via least squares from prevalence data.
AI.conclusion: Provides a coherent framework for teachers to integrate model assumptions, units, simulation, and inference in introductory infectious disease modeling education.

title: Learning Cardiac Features: ECG Biometrics Across Time and~Exercise
summary: Electrocardiograms (ECGs) carry subject-specific patterns enabling reliable individual discrimination, forming the basis of ECG biometrics. Beyond authentication, this paradigm holds significant potential to secure sensitive cardiac data and to serve as a pretext task in self-supervised learning. Yet, most studies remain confined to singlesession, resting data, leaving robustness to temporal and physiological variations largely untested. We address this gap by evaluating ECG biometrics under realistic conditions involving exercise-induced stress and cross-session variability. A Siamese ResNet with late multi-lead fusion strategy is trained on a large ECG dataset extracted from cardiopulmonary exercise tests and evaluated with a exercise-and time-aware protocol, as well as on public benchmarks. This first extensive assessment of ECG biometrics under combined physiological and temporal variability achieves an intra-session rest-to-peak EER of 1.7% and stateof-the-art 3.9% on the CYBHi dataset. Findings support the presence of an intrinsic cardiac signature resilient to physiological and temporal drift.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates ECG biometrics under realistic conditions involving exercise-induced stress and cross-session variability, using a Siamese ResNet with late multi-lead fusion, achieving strong discrimination performance.
AI.motivation: Most ECG biometrics studies are limited to single-session, resting data, leaving robustness to temporal and physiological variations untested. The authors aim to bridge this gap to support authentication, securing sensitive cardiac data, and self-supervised learning pretext tasks.
AI.method: A Siamese ResNet with a late multi-lead fusion strategy is trained on a large ECG dataset from cardiopulmonary exercise tests and evaluated with an exercise-and-time-aware protocol plus public benchmarks.
AI.result: The approach achieves an intra-session rest-to-peak EER of 1.7% and state-of-the-art 3.9% on the CYBHi dataset.
AI.conclusion: Findings support the presence of an intrinsic cardiac signature resilient to physiological and temporal drift, indicating ECG biometrics can remain robust under realistic variability.

title: BrainWideBench: Benchmarking large-scale pretraining and across-animal transfer in multi-region neural recordings
summary: Advances in large-scale neural recording have made it possible to collect data across many animals and distributed brain regions, raising the question of whether this scale can be exploited to learn general-purpose neural representations transferable across diverse downstream tasks. Yet, progress toward this goal has been limited by fragmented evaluation protocols and a narrow focus on individual task domains. Here, we present BrainWideBench, a benchmark for evaluating across-animal transfer on multi-region neural recordings, built on the International Brain Laboratory Brainwide Map dataset of neural and behavioral recordings spanning 276 brain regions from 139 mice performing a sensory-guided decision-making task. The benchmark is organized around three complementary task suites that evaluate whether learned representations support downstream decoding of behavior, can predict masked or future neural activity, and can recover biologically meaningful anatomical organization. With this benchmark, we systematically evaluate pretraining methods across transfer settings, including finetuning on downstream objectives and zero-shot generalization to unseen animals. Our results confirm pretraining improves performance over matched single-session baselines, but we show current methods exhibit heterogeneity in transfer capabilities: gains depend strongly on the alignment between pretraining objectives and downstream tasks. No single approach performs uniformly well across all three suites, and most methods are designed to only address a subset of them. Together, these findings suggest that learning representations that jointly generalize across behavior, dynamics, and anatomy remains an open challenge. By providing a unified and reproducible evaluation suite, BrainWideBench establishes a framework for measuring progress toward general-purpose models of the mouse brain.

AI.tldr: BrainWideBench is a new benchmark for evaluating cross-animal transfer of neural representations on multi-region recordings from the IBL Brainwide Map (276 regions, 139 mice). It reveals that no current pretraining method generalizes uniformly across behavior decoding, neural prediction, and anatomical recovery.
AI.motivation: Large-scale neural recording now spans many animals and distributed brain regions, raising the possibility of learning general-purpose representations transferable across tasks. However, progress has been hindered by fragmented evaluation protocols and a narrow focus on individual task domains, making it hard to measure genuine transfer.
AI.method: The authors introduce BrainWideBench, built on the IBL Brainwide Map dataset (276 brain regions, 139 mice, sensory-guided decision-making task). It organizes evaluation into three complementary task suites: (1) downstream behavior decoding, (2) prediction of masked or future neural activity, and (3) recovery of biological anatomical organization. Pretraining methods are systematically tested under finetuning and zero-shot generalization to unseen animals.
AI.result: Pretraining improves performance over matched single-session baselines. However, transfer capabilities are heterogeneous: gains depend strongly on alignment between pretraining objectives and downstream tasks, no single approach performs uniformly well across all three suites, and most methods target only a subset of them.
AI.conclusion: Learning representations that jointly generalize across behavior, dynamics, and anatomy remains an open challenge. BrainWideBench offers a unified, reproducible suite for measuring progress toward general-purpose models of the mouse brain.
